claim: The spec's own design principle is "Reduction without a relevance signal is truncation, and truncation is only defensible against a budget." The head-only ladder is that budget-driven truncation, and its first rung is `headLines: 400`. But the spec's stated problem is that refuters saw ~4% of a 301506-byte bundle (≈12935 bytes ≈ ~3200 lines of source). A 400-line head on a file that is, say, 3000 lines long retains ~13% of that file — the same order of magnitude of loss the spec is trying to eliminate. The spec justifies the top rung as "high enough that the first rung is a real attempt at keeping files usable," but 400 lines is not "usable" for the stale-reuse defect class the spec itself names (a helper's definition "can sit anywhere in a file and a 100-line head often misses it"). The ladder's top rung is therefore not a meaningful retention attempt; it is a coarser version of the 12-line truncation the spec condemns. The only rung that actually restores the spec's goal (whole-file retention) is the stand-down itself — and the head-only ladder only fires when the stand-down's payload overflows the window, i.e. precisely when the spec cannot deliver its goal. So in the regime where the ladder matters, it delivers a degraded context with no architectural argument for why 400 is the right first cut rather than, say, 2000 or "the largest head that fits."
evidence: Spec §3 "The head ladder's rung values" ("`[400, 200, 100, 50, 24, 12]` is a judgement, not a measurement"); §3 "What the window-targeted trim does when the anchor yield is zero" ("Head retention rather than dropping whole files, because an elided file body still carries `elisionMarker`'s in-payload sentinel"); §6 "Head retention or whole-file dropping" ("a helper's definition can sit anywhere in a file and a 100-line head often misses it"); §1 "Problem statement" (the 301506→12935 measurement).
predicted_consequence: On the first over-window spec-review payload, the refuters receive a 400-line head of each file — a context that is still ~87% elided — and the spec's own success criterion (refuters see the whole file) is not met in exactly the case (large bundle + declared window) where the head-only ladder is the load-bearing path. The operator has no way to know 400 was the wrong first rung, because the note only says "tightened to head-lines 400," not "400 lines is 13% of this file."

claim: The spec's §4 "Failure modes" first item concedes that "A spec that quotes a unified-diff hunk defeats the predicate." A spec body containing `@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@` inside a fenced block opens a hunk in `parseDiffTouched`, which collects identifiers from the quoted body. If any of those identifiers hit a context file, `filesAnchored > 0`, the stand-down does not fire, and every file is head-reduced to 12 lines — the exact bug the spec is fixing. The spec says "How you would know: the `FAFF-915 context trim` note still appears on a spec-review lens after this lands. What it means: narrow, not abandon. The next step would be a yield floor rather than a yield of zero, and that needs a measurement this ticket does not have." But this is an architectural objection, not a taste one: the spec's central predicate is a binary (zero vs non-zero) that is trivially defeated by the most common way a spec discusses code (quoting a diff hunk). The spec explicitly defers the fix ("a yield floor") to a future ticket "that needs a measurement this ticket does not have." This means the spec ships a predicate that is known to be wrong for a realistic input class, with the correction explicitly out of scope. The architectural soundness of the approach depends on the assumption that specs will not quote diff hunks, which the spec itself does not establish and which is contradicted by the fact that the spec under review (FAFF-1051) is about a diff-anchored trim and will naturally contain `@@` examples in its own prose.
evidence: Spec §4 "Failure modes" first bullet ("A spec that quotes a unified-diff hunk defeats the predicate... The next step would be a yield floor rather than a yield of zero, and that needs a measurement this ticket does not have"); §3 "Where the stand-down predicate is measured" (the predicate is `filesAnchored == 0`); `parseDiffTouched` in `review-call.mjs` (recognises `@@` headers and collects identifiers from `+`/`-` body lines regardless of whether they are inside a markdown fence).
predicted_consequence: The first spec that quotes a diff hunk (which FAFF-1051's own spec text does, in its §4 "How the pieces connect" and §5 "Scenarios") will not stand down; its context will be head-reduced to 12 lines per file; the refuters will again see ~4% of the context; and the operator will see the `FAFF-915 context trim` note and have no in-band signal that the stand-down was supposed to fire but was defeated by a quoted hunk. The spec's own DONE criteria do not cover this case, so the build agent will ship the binary predicate and the defect will be discovered only in production.

claim: The spec widens `TrimReport` with `reason`, `filesTotal`, and `filesAnchored`, and adds `onNoAnchorYield` to `trimContextFiles`'s options. The DONE criteria that read these fields are: "the report carries `reason`... and `reason` is one of `disabled`, `under-threshold`, `no-anchor-yield`, `trimmed`" and "`reason == "trimmed"` if and only if `trimmed == true`, asserted directly." But the only behavioural consumer of `reason` is `main`'s stderr note (which fires on `reason == "no-anchor-yield"` and `reason == "trimmed"`). The `filesTotal` and `filesAnchored` fields are read by no DONE criterion other than the stand-down note's text ("naming the file count and the byte count"). The `onNoAnchorYield` option is read by `tightenToTarget` (which passes `"head-reduce"`), but `tightenToTarget` is the only caller that sets it, and `main`'s byte-gated call site never sets it (it uses the default `"stand-down"`). So the option is a one-caller knob that could be a private branch inside `trimContextFiles` rather than a public option. The architectural cost is small, but the spec's own §6 "Widening the report, or a separate return value?" argues for widening on the grounds that "the report already exists, has exactly one consumer (`main`), and the added fields are additive" — which is true, but the `onNoAnchorYield` option is not a report field, it is a behavioural switch, and it is not justified by the same argument. A simpler design would keep `onNoAnchorYield` private to `tightenToTarget`'s call (passing a flag that `trimContextFiles` interprets internally) rather than exposing it as a public option that future callers can set to `"head-reduce"` and get a different reduction semantics they did not ask for.
evidence: Spec §3 "Types" (`INTERFACE trimContextFiles(opts)` with `opts.onNoAnchorYield: Enum{ "stand-down", "head-reduce" }`); §6 "Widening the report, or a separate return value?"; DONE "From WHAT (types and interfaces)" (the report-field assertions); DONE "From HOW (behaviour)" ("`trimContextFiles({ onNoAnchorYield: "head-reduce" })` on a zero-yield bundle head-reduces every file above `minFileBytes`").
predicted_consequence: A future caller that passes `onNoAnchorYield: "head-reduce"` to `trimContextFiles` for a non-zero-yield bundle gets head-reduction semantics it did not intend (the option is only meaningful in the zero-yield regime, but the spec does not say what happens when it is set on a non-zero-yield bundle — the Pseudocode step 5 only checks `filesAnchored == 0 AND opts.onNoAnchorYield == "stand-down"`, so a non-zero-yield bundle with `onNoAnchorYield: "head-reduce"` falls through to step 6 and is reduced normally, which is fine, but the option's name implies it controls the no-anchor-yield behaviour, not the general reduction behaviour). The blast radius is small, but the option is a public seam that the spec does not need.

claim: The spec's edge-cases section states that "an early rung can leave a small file identical to its input while reducing a large one" and that "the search's minimum tracking already tolerates it," but no DONE item or scenario asserts this behaviour. A build could silently break the small-file path in the head-only regime (e.g., by emitting a zero-count elision marker, or by miscounting lines when `headLines` exceeds the file's line count) and every named AC would still pass.
evidence: Edge case "A file shorter than the rung's head lines" in §4 (HOW → Edge cases); no corresponding item in §8 DONE.
predicted_consequence: A regression in `headReduce`'s handling of files shorter than the rung's head lines (e.g., emitting a marker with a negative or zero elided count, or corrupting the file's text) would not be caught by any test the spec requires, because the existing `headReduce` tests in `test/adversarial-call.test.mjs` only exercise the `headLines < fileLines.length` path and the `headLines >= fileLines.length` path at the boundary, not the head-only ladder's specific interaction with small files at multiple rung values.
